d: The creation of the world, Eden, and the first human choices.
Two brothers, the generations beyond Eden, and a world awaiting Noah.
Noah, the ark, the flood, the dove, and the covenant marked by the rainbow.
The nations after the flood, the tower at Babel, and the family line that leads to Abram.
Abram's calling, journeys, promises, Hagar, and the covenant of Abraham and Sarah.
Abraham and Sarah, Sodom, the birth of Isaac, and the difficult test at Moriah.

t: A Wife for Isaac and Two Twin Brothers
d: Sarah's burial, Rebekah and Isaac, Esau and Jacob, and a blessing gained by deceit.
Jacob's journey to Haran, his growing family, a night of wrestling, and reunion with Esau.
Dinah, the losses in Jacob's family, Joseph's betrayal, and the account of Judah and Tamar.
Joseph's life in Egypt, imprisonment, the dreams, and the plan for famine.
Joseph's brothers return to Egypt, Benjamin is tested, and Joseph reveals himself.
Jacob's family settles in Egypt, final blessings and burial, and Joseph's farewell.
Israel’s oppression, Moses’ rescue and calling, and his return to Egypt.
Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh, the heavier labor, and the first nine plagues.
Passover, departure from Egypt, the sea crossing, and the first wilderness waters.
Manna and quail in the wilderness, water from the rock, Amalek’s attack, and Jethro’s counsel.
Thunder at Sinai, the Ten Commandments, the laws of daily life, and the covenant sealed with blood.
The pattern shown on the mountain: the ark, the tent, the priestly garments, and the craftsman God named.
The golden calf, Moses’ intercession, God’s name proclaimed on the mountain, and Moses returning with a radiant face.
The tabernacle built as commanded, set up on the first day of the year, and filled with the glory of the LORD.
The offerings at the tent: burnt, grain, peace, sin, and guilt, and a pattern of atonement that reaches from a bull to a handful of flour.

t: The Priests Begin, and Fire Falls Twice
d: Aaron and his sons are ordained, fire falls on the offering, and then fire falls again on Nadab and Abihu.

t: Clean, Unclean, and the Day That Cleanses All
d: Clean and unclean in food, birth, skin, and houses, and the one day a year when atonement reaches behind the veil.

t: A Holy People in Daily Life
d: Holiness moves into daily life: blood, family, wages, courts, the foreigner, and the men at the altar.
God’s calendar of feasts, the land’s Sabbath and Jubilee, one hard court case, and the choice between blessing and exile.
Israel is counted as an army and camped in order around the tent, and the Levites are set apart to carry what no one may touch.

t: Blessing, Trumpets, and the First March
d: The camp is blessed, given trumpets and a cloud to follow, and takes its first steps on the road.
Three days in, the complaints begin: craving at Kibroth-hattaavah, then Miriam and Aaron turn on Moses.
Twelve spies see the same land and bring back two reports, and a generation is sentenced to the wilderness.

t: Korah and the Staff That Blossomed
d: Korah's rebellion is swallowed by the ground, Aaron stands between the living and the dead, and a dead staff blossoms.

t: Water, a Serpent, and the End of the Old Road
d: Miriam and Aaron die, Moses strikes the rock, and the new generation wins its first land east of the Jordan.

t: Balaam and the Fall at Peor
d: Balak hires Balaam to curse Israel and gets blessings instead, but at Peor the camp wounds itself.
A new generation is counted, five daughters change the inheritance law, Joshua is commissioned, and the book ends facing the river.
Moses retells the journey for the children who did not live it, from Horeb and the spies to the sentence, the long bypass, and his own refused plea to cross the Jordan.
The commandments are given again, the Shema is taught, and Moses warns against forgetting when the houses are full, retelling the golden calf from his side of the mountain.

t: One Altar, and Laws for Settled Life
d: Worship gathers to one chosen place, false prophets are tested, and the tithe, the seventh-year release, and the three feasts order the life of a settled people.

t: Judges, a King, and a Prophet to Come
d: Courts are fenced with witnesses, the future king is placed under a book he must copy by hand, the prophet like Moses is promised, and refuge cities and the laws of war are set down.

t: Life in the Land, Case by Case
d: The covenant at the size of a household: an unsolved murder, a lost ox, a cloak returned by sunset, wages paid the same day, honest weights, and the memory of Amalek.

t: Firstfruits, Two Mountains, and the Choice Set Down
d: A farmer recites the whole story over a basket of firstfruits, two mountains answer Amen to the curses, blessings and curses are set in full, and the covenant is renewed in Moab.

t: Choose Life, a Song, and the Mountain
d: The way back from exile, the word very near, choose life, Joshua commissioned, the Song of Moses, the blessings of the tribes, and Moses on Nebo, seeing the land he will not enter.
God commissions Moses' assistant, two spies find faith inside Jericho, and the Jordan stops at flood stage for a nation's crossing.

t: Gilgal, Jericho, and the Sin in the Camp
d: A circumcised camp, the last manna, a silent march around Jericho, one man's hidden theft, and the law read between two mountains.

t: The Gibeonite Covenant and the Long Day
d: A treaty won by moldy bread, an oath kept anyway, an all-night march to defend it, and a day longer than any before or since.

t: The North Taken, and the List of Kings
d: Chariots at the waters of Merom, Hazor burned, a long war honestly recorded, and thirty-one kings counted like stones.

t: The Land Divided, and Caleb's Mountain
d: An old general, an older promise, an eighty-five-year-old asking for the giants' hill country, and Judah's hundred towns.

t: Lots at Shiloh and the Cities of Refuge
d: Five sisters collect on a ruling, Joseph's sons are told to clear their own forest, forty-eight Levitical towns, and a verdict: not one promise failed.
A homecoming, an imposing altar, a nation arming for civil war, and an embassy that chose questions before swords.
Two farewell speeches, God's own voice retelling the whole story, a vow priced before it was accepted, and three burials at Shechem.

t: A Generation That Did Not Know
d: Joshua is gone, the conquest stalls tribe by tribe, and the angel at Bochim names the cycle that will run the whole book.

t: Othniel, Ehud, and the Left Hand
d: The first two deliverers: Othniel the model judge, and a left-handed Benjamite with a hidden dagger and a locked door.

t: Deborah and the Song of Victory
d: A prophetess under a palm tree, nine hundred iron chariots in the mud, and a song that tells what the battle meant.
A frightened man threshing wheat in a winepress is called a mighty man of valor, and his army is sent home until three hundred remain.
Gideon refuses a crown and builds a snare of gold, and his son buys a kingship with temple silver and one stone.
The outcast son argues like a statesman, wins his war, and meets the price of a careless vow at his own door.

t: Samson: The Riddle and the Foxes
d: Announced before his birth and set apart from the womb, Samson begins a deliverance fought mostly as a private feud.
The secret is pressed out of him on Delilah's lap, and the blind prisoner prays once more between the pillars.
A stolen fortune becomes an idol, a Levite is hired at ten shekels a year, and a tribe steals a shrine on its way north.

t: Gibeah, and the War That Cost a Tribe
d: A crime in Benjamin summons all Israel to Mizpah, and the oaths sworn there nearly erase a tribe from the nation.

t: Where You Go, I Will Go
d: A famine, three funerals in Moab, and a daughter-in-law who will not go home.
A gleaner finds a field, a protector, and the first news of a redeemer.
A midnight proposal, a morning at the gate, and a baby who changes the genealogy.

t: Hannah, and the Boy Who Heard God
d: Hannah's prayer, a vow kept, and a boy who learns to answer God in the night at Shiloh.
The ark carried into battle and captured, Dagon fallen, and a stone of help raised at Mizpah.
Israel demands a king, Samuel warns what a king will take, and Saul is found among the baggage.

t: The Kingdom Renewed, and the First Crack
d: Jabesh rescued, Samuel's farewell, and Saul's unlawful sacrifice at Gilgal.

t: Jonathan's Climb, and the Sentence on Saul
d: Two men climb a cliff in faith, and a king spares what God devoted to destruction.

t: The Shepherd Anointed, and the Giant
d: A youngest son anointed in secret, and a shepherd who runs toward Goliath.

t: Ten Thousands, and the Son of the King
d: A victory song, three spears, a covenant, and arrows by the stone Ezel.
Nob, Gath, the cave of Adullam, and a king spared in the dark at En-gedi.

t: Abigail, and the Night at Endor
d: A wise woman stops a massacre, a spear taken twice, and a king's last night at Endor.

t: Ziklag in Ashes, and the Fall of Saul
d: Everything lost and recovered at Ziklag, and the death of Saul and Jonathan on Gilboa.

t: The Lament for Saul and Jonathan
d: A messenger, a crown, an execution, and the Song of the Bow taught to all Judah.

t: King of Judah, War with the House of Saul
d: Hebron, the pool of Gibeon, Asahel's death, Abner's defection and murder, and a throne left open.

t: King Over All Israel, and Jerusalem
d: The tribes covenant at Hebron, a taunted city taken, and the ark brought up past Uzzah's fall.
A king who would build God a house receives a house instead, and the wars that followed it.
A crippled prince seated at the king's table, and a kindness across the border answered with humiliation and war.
A king who stayed home, a soldier who would not, a parable of a lamb, and a sentence on a house.
A sister wronged, a king's silence, two years of waiting, and a wise woman from Tekoa.
Stolen hearts at the gate, a barefoot flight over Olivet, two counsels, and a prayer answered by delay.

t: The Forest of Ephraim, and a Father's Cry
d: Twenty thousand in the forest, a king between two gates, a hard return, and Sheba's trumpet.
A famine and a mother's vigil, the great song, the honor roll, and a threshing floor bought at full price.

t: The Old King and the Contested Throne
d: An old king who cannot keep warm, a throne seized at a feast, and a kingdom established at a price.
A dream at Gibeon, a sword over a living child, and a kingdom laid out in ledgers.
Cedars from Lebanon, stones dressed in silence, and a house of gold built in seven years.
The ark comes up, the cloud fills the house, and a king prays for days he will not see.

t: The Queen of Sheba and the Turn
d: A queen's visit, a river of gold, and the slow turn of a king's heart.
A harsh answer at Shechem, two golden calves, a lion by the road, and bronze shields.
Reign by reign the two kingdoms slide, until Ahab arrives and the scale breaks.
A shut sky, a widow's jar, fire on Carmel, and rain the size of a man's hand.
A broom tree, a whisper on Horeb, two wars Ahab did not earn, and a verdict in disguise.

t: Naboth's Vineyard and the Last Battle
d: A vineyard refused, a king in sackcloth, one prophet against four hundred, and an arrow drawn at random.

t: Fire from Heaven, and the Mantle Falls
d: Elijah is taken up in the whirlwind, and Elisha takes up the mantle, the Jordan, and the work.
Three kings march against Moab, run out of water, and get a word about ditches.

t: Oil, Bread, and a Son Raised
d: A widow's oil, a Shunammite's son, poison drawn from a pot, and bread that outlasts the count.
Aram's commander is healed in the Jordan, and the prophet's servant takes the disease he tried to sell.
Blind raiders are feasted, a starving city hears tomorrow's prices, and four lepers find an empty camp.
The Shunammite gets her land back from the king, and Elisha weeps over the king Hazael will become.
Jehu is anointed in secret and drives to Jezreel, where two kings and a queen meet Elijah's word.

t: The Purge, and the Hidden Child
d: Jehu finishes Ahab's house and Baal's temple, and in Jerusalem a child survives a queen's purge.

t: The Temple Repaired, and Elisha's Last Arrow
d: Joash repairs the temple, Israel dwindles under Hazael, and Elisha's last arrow sets a king's limit.

t: The Quick Kings and the Foreign Altar
d: Amaziah's pride, Jeroboam's prosperity, a line of murdered kings, and Ahaz's foreign altar.
Samaria falls after three years of siege, and the book reads out the verdict it has compiled for centuries.
Hezekiah breaks Assyria's script with silence, sackcloth, and a letter spread before the LORD.
Hezekiah gains fifteen years and shows Babylon everything; Manasseh spends fifty-five undoing him.
A lost book is found in the temple, and Josiah's reform runs back through three centuries of altars.
Jehoiachin surrenders, Zedekiah is blinded, the temple burns, and the book ends at a Babylonian table.
Called to preach to Nineveh, Jonah runs the other way, and a storm, a crew of praying sailors, and a great fish carry him back.
Jonah preaches five words, the enemy city repents to a man, and the prophet sits outside its walls angry at God's mercy.
A shepherd from Tekoa carries eight oracles in one formula, and the ring of judgment closes nation by nation until it lands on Israel.
Election means exposure: the lion roars, Samaria's luxury is summoned before witnesses, and five disasters end on the same refrain.
A funeral lament sung to a living nation, the open door of Seek Me and live, and justice rolling on like a river.

t: The Plumb Line and the Priest
d: Amos argues God out of two visions, the plumb line ends the arguing, and at Bethel the king's priest meets the shepherd's only credential.

t: No Escape, and the Booth of David
d: The Lord stands by the altar and there is nowhere to hide; then the book turns: the fallen tent of David raised and a people planted for good.
A prophet is told to marry his sermon, and his children's names preach it.
God pleads His case against Israel as a husband, and ends it with a betrothal.

t: Bought Back, and No Knowledge of God
d: Hosea buys back his wife, and the trial of the land opens on a missing knowledge.

t: The Moth and the Morning Mist
d: A moth, a lion who withdraws, and a repentance song answered by morning mist.
An oven of kings, a silly dove between empires, and the law of the whirlwind.
The watchman is called a fool, and the luxuriant vine meets the plow.
God remembers teaching His child to walk, and His heart turns within Him.
The final indictment, the ransom questions at Sheol's edge, and love given freely.
The lawsuit opens: heaven and earth are called to witness against a rebellious city.

t: The Mountain and the Daughters of Zion
d: The mountain of the LORD rises over a land full of idols, and the daughters of Zion parade through judgment.
A love song for a vineyard turns into six woes, and fire answers the diagnosis.
In the year Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the King, is cleansed by a coal, and meets the first sign-child.
A second sign-child, a flood Judah chose, a stone to stumble on, and then a great light and a child.
Assyria is the rod in God's hand, and the rod does not know it.
From Jesse's stump, a shoot; from the shoot, a world at peace and a second exodus.
The burdens open: Babylon falls, its king is taunted in Sheol, and God's purpose stands over the whole earth.

t: My Heart Cries Out for Moab
d: The prophet weeps over Moab, Damascus and Ephraim fade together, and gifts come up from Cush.
The LORD rides into Egypt, and the burden ends with Egypt called My people.
From the watchtower: Babylon fallen, Dumah's unanswered night, Shebna displaced, and Tyre's seventy years.
The whole earth under judgment, and on the mountain a feast that swallows death.
A song of the strong city, an honest prayer, Leviathan slain, and the great shofar gathering.
A drunken garland, vomit-covered tables, a covenant with death, and a cornerstone measured true.
Salvation by repentance and rest, refused for horses; Assyria burns at the breath of God.
The last woes fall on Egypt-trusters and the destroyer, and eyes behold the King in His beauty.
Edom's uncreation answers to a blooming desert and the highway of holiness.
Sennacherib's spokesman preaches surrender at the aqueduct, and Hezekiah takes the letter into the temple.
Fifteen years added, a king's own writing, and Babylonian envoys shown everything.
Comfort for the exile: a voice in the wilderness, a God beyond measure, strength for those who wait.
The courtroom of the nations: God speaks first to His servant, do not fear.
Here is My Servant, who will not break a bruised reed; Israel, blind and plundered, is named servant too.
You are Mine: witnesses called, former things forgotten, transgressions blotted out for God's own sake.
The idol factory toured at length, and Cyrus named a shepherd before he is born.
Cyrus, His anointed; clay warned before the potter; Babylon's gods carried away on animals.
Babylon's queen steps down to the dust, and Israel is told to leave her with singing.
The Servant speaks for himself, Zion's name is found inscribed on God's palms, and the student's song follows.
Three Listens, the cup of wrath lifted from Jerusalem, and beautiful feet on the mountains.
The suffering Servant, nearly whole; then the barren woman sings and the market opens free.
Foreigners and eunuchs welcomed, watchmen asleep, and the fast God chose.
Confession in the dark, then sunrise: arise, shine, for your light has come.

t: The Year of the LORD's Favor
d: The year of the LORD's favor, watchmen who never keep silent, and a city with new names.
The warrior comes from Edom alone, and the book's longest prayer remembers everything.

t: New Heavens and a New Earth
d: New heavens and a new earth; the book ends with worship and a sight the retelling will not soften.
Samaria is sentenced, and the prophet laments barefoot as the incurable wound reaches Jerusalem's gate.

t: They Plot Evil on Their Beds
d: Fields are seized at dawn by men who plotted at night, and the chapter ends with the Breaker opening the gate.
Rulers who devour, prophets for hire, and Zion plowed like a field.

t: The Mountain of the House of the LORD
d: The mountain of the LORD rises, the lame are gathered, and the nations become sheaves on the threshing floor.
Out of small Bethlehem, a shepherd ruler; in that day, every false trust is cut off.
God pleads His case before the mountains, and the answer is justice, mercy, and a humble walk.

t: But as for Me, I Will Look to the LORD
d: The godly have vanished and enemies fill the house, but Micah takes his post: I will look to the LORD.

t: Who Is a God Like You?
d: Walls rebuilt, the flock shepherded home, and sins cast into the depths of the sea.

t: The LORD Is Slow to Anger
d: Before the sentence, the character of God: avenging and slow to anger, a stronghold for those who trust Him.
The fall narrated as scene: red shields, the river gates open, the pool draining, the lions' den empty.

t: Woe to the City of Blood
d: The charges read out, the harlot exposed, and Thebes argued as the precedent Nineveh cannot escape.
Figs for fortresses, locusts for an empire, sleeping shepherds, and a wound with no healing.
The word comes in Josiah's days, and its first sentence sweeps the whole earth, creation named in reverse, before the hand turns to Judah.

t: I Will Search Jerusalem with Lamps
d: The Day arrives as sound at the gates, then as lamplight in the dark corners, finding the men who settled around the belief that God would do nothing.
A shameful nation is told to gather and seek humility inside a perhaps, while the word walks the compass: Philistia, Moab and Ammon, Cush, and Nineveh last.
The woe comes home to Jerusalem, every office corrupt under a God who kept His dawn appointments; then, past the fire, pure lips for the peoples and a meek remnant left in the city.

t: He Will Rejoice over You with Singing
d: The book ends in song: the punishment taken away, the King in her midst, and God rejoicing over His gathered people with gladness, quieting them with His love, singing.

t: Before I Formed You in the Womb
d: A boy from Anathoth is told he was known before he was formed, and is given a commission with two halves: uproot and plant.
Israel is charged with two evils in one act: forsaking the fountain of living water, and hewing out broken cisterns that hold nothing.
The call to return runs through the chapter like a refrain, while the north is summoned home and the valley fills with what Israel has loved.
The foe from the north is named, the watchmen cry out, and Jeremiah sees creation itself run backward over his people.

t: If You Can Find a Single Person
d: God offers to pardon the city for one honest person, and Jeremiah reports what his search of the streets found.
The bellows blow and the lead is spent, but the wicked are not drawn off; the LORD names them rejected silver.
Standing in the gate of the LORD's house, Jeremiah tells the worshipers not to trust in the temple chant, and the sermon nearly ends him.

t: Is There No Balm in Gilead?
d: The daughter of God's people is wounded, there is no balm and no physician, and the harvest passes with no rescue.
Jeremiah wishes his head were waters and his eyes a fountain, for a people whose tongues bend like bows to shoot lies.
The idols of the nations are scarecrows in a cucumber patch, set against the God who made the earth by His power.
Jeremiah proclaims the broken covenant through Judah, and his own town of Anathoth plots to kill him for it.
Jeremiah pleads his righteous case and asks why the treacherous thrive; the answer sends him from a footrace to horses.
A new loincloth buried by the Euphrates comes back ruined, and the pride of Judah is read aloud from its rot.
The land mourns without water, the prophets lie about peace, and God tells Jeremiah not to pray for this people.
Not even Moses and Samuel could turn God now, and Jeremiah's own complaint is answered with a call to return himself.
Jeremiah is forbidden a wife, a funeral, and a feast in that place, three empty rooms preaching the withdrawal of peace.

t: The Tree Planted by the Waters
d: A shrub in the desert and a tree by the waters are set side by side, and the Sabbath is preached at the gates of the city.
At the potter's wheel a spoiled vessel is remade, and Judah answers the offer with a shrug: that is in vain.
A flask is smashed in the valley and a priest is renamed Terror on Every Side, in the sermon that runs from Topheth to the stocks.
Jeremiah accuses God of deceiving him, cannot hold the fire in, sings one verse, and curses the day he was born.

t: The Way of Life and the Way of Death
d: With Babylon at the door, Jeremiah sets before the city the way of life and the way of death, and tells the king's messengers God's answer.

t: Woe to the Kings of the House
d: Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Coniah are judged one by one, and a cedar palace is measured against the justice of Josiah.
False shepherds are sentenced, a righteous Branch is promised, and dreams are weighed as straw against the wheat of the word.
Two baskets before the temple sort the nation: good figs carried into exile, bad figs left behind with Zedekiah.
The sermon is dated and sealed: seventy years for Babylon's rule, then the cup of wrath poured for every nation in turn.
The temple sermon is retried as a capital case, and the elders save Jeremiah with the hundred-year-old precedent of Micah.
Jeremiah wears a yoke before the nations' envoys, Hananiah breaks it in the temple, and God replaces the wood with iron.
Jeremiah writes to Babylon: build houses, plant gardens, seek the city's welfare, and do not listen to your prophets there.
The book of consolation opens with a writing command, an incurable wound, and a promise that Jacob's trouble ends in rest.

t: Rachel Weeping, and a New Covenant
d: Rachel weeps at Ramah and is answered, road markers are set for the way home, and a new covenant is promised with the law on the heart.
While the siege closes in, Jeremiah buys his cousin's field at Anathoth and jars the deed, because fields will be bought in the land again.
From the prison court comes the invitation: call to Me and I will answer you, and tell you great and hidden things.
Jerusalem frees its Hebrew slaves by covenant under siege, then takes the freedom back, and God proclaims a liberty of another kind.

t: The Rechabites and the Burned Scroll
d: The Rechabites keep a dead father's command for 250 years; Jehoiakim burns the scroll column by column, and God dictates it again, with additions.

t: The Cistern and the Secret King
d: Jeremiah is arrested as a deserter, lowered into a mud cistern, lifted out on ropes padded with rags, and summoned to a secret audience.
Jerusalem falls in a chapter of plain record, and the spoil-of-war promise is paid by name to a prophet and a Cushite servant.
Gedaliah gathers the remnant at Mizpah and is murdered at his own table; the rescued captives camp at Geruth Chimham facing a decision of fear.
The remnant swears to obey, waits ten days, hears stay, and marches to Egypt anyway, carrying Jeremiah to his last recorded sermon.
The book's smallest chapter answers its scribe: do not seek great things for yourself; your life will be granted you as a spoil of war.
The nations section opens: Egypt routed at Carchemish is sent to Gilead for a balm that cannot heal her, and the sword is addressed over the Philistine coast.
Moab, settled like wine on its dregs and never poured out, is poured at last, and God Himself wails over the nation He is judging.

t: Milcom, Esau, and the Small Nations
d: Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, and Elam are judged in one chapter; two of the five end with restoration, and Edom does not.
The banner is lifted and nothing held back: Babylon is captured, Bel is shamed, and Israel and Judah come weeping together to ask the way to Zion.
God addresses His war club, sings the Creator hymn over Babylon a second time, and hears Zion's complaint entered into the record.
God pleads Zion's case, Bel is made to spew out what he swallowed, and Seraiah sinks the Babylon scroll in the Euphrates on a stone.
The appendix retells the fall as record, counts the exile by name and number, and ends on a pardoned king dining at Babylon's table for life.
Habakkuk complains about violence and broken courts in Judah, and God answers with the Chaldeans.

t: Will He Continue to Slay Nations Without Mercy?
d: The prophet protests that a holy God is silent while the wicked swallow the righteous, then takes his post to wait.

t: The Righteous Will Live by Faith
d: God commands the vision written on tablets: an appointed time, and the righteous living by faith.

t: Woe to Him Who Amasses What Is Not His
d: The plundered nations sing five woes over the conqueror, ending in the silence of the temple.

t: Yet I Will Rejoice in the LORD
d: Habakkuk prays: God comes in glory, the prophet trembles, and rejoices over empty fields.
God summons the nations against proud Edom, nested in the cliffs and certain no one can bring it down.
The charges are read: on Jerusalem's worst day, brother Edom gloated, looted, and hunted the fugitives.

t: The Kingdom Will Belong to the LORD
d: The measure returns on every nation, Zion is restored, and the book ends: the kingdom belongs to the LORD.
The widowed city sits empty, stretches out her hands, and finds no one to comfort her.

t: The Lord Is Like an Enemy
d: The second poem names the attacker, and it is not Babylon: the LORD has bent His bow against His own city.
One unnamed sufferer tells what affliction felt like from inside, and finds hope by an act of memory.
The same voice turns from endurance to examination: confession, the pit, and a God who draws near.
The fourth poem holds what the city was up against what it is, and finds her punishment has a limit.
The survivors pray the inventory of their disgrace aloud, and the book ends on an unanswered unless.

t: The Glory by the River Kebar
d: By a canal in Babylon the heavens open over a young priest in exile, and the glory he sees will follow him for the rest of the book.
Facedown before the glory, Ezekiel is stood on his feet, named son of man, and fed his message on a scroll written on both sides.

t: The Watchman and the Silenced Prophet
d: Seven days of stunned silence end with a job title, a charter of life and death, and a prophet bound and mute in his own house.

t: The Brick, the Bread, and the Hair
d: The silenced prophet preaches with a brick, a scale, a cooking fire, and a razor, acting out Jerusalem's siege in his own body.
The sermons begin: a word against the mountains, a remnant promised through the ruin, and an alarm bell that rings one word, the end.
Taken by the hair to Jerusalem, Ezekiel tours the temple in a vision and watches the abominations grow worse room by room.
Six executioners enter the city, a man in linen marks the foreheads of those who grieve, and the glory begins to move.

t: The Pot, the Promise, and the Mountain
d: At the east gate the glory pauses over leaders who call the city a cooking pot, then the promise of a new heart is given to the exiles instead.
Ezekiel packs exile baggage by day and digs through his own wall at dusk, while two proverbs of delay get their answer.

t: Whitewash and Idols in the Heart
d: Whitewashed walls, magic charms, and elders with idols in their hearts: the word turns on false prophets and compromised worship.

t: The Foundling Who Became a Queen
d: A useless vine and a foundling bride tell Jerusalem's whole story, rescue, splendor, betrayal, and a covenant God still remembers.

t: Two Eagles and a Tender Sprig
d: Two eagles, a vine, and a broken oath decode Zedekiah's rebellion, then God plants a tender sprig of His own on the high mountain.
The sour-grapes proverb is put to death in a family of three generations, and God asks whether He takes any pleasure in the death of the wicked.
A funeral song for living kings, lion cubs caged and a scepter vine burned, closes with the prophet's complaint that no one hears more than parables.

t: For the Sake of My Name
d: The elders come to ask and get a history lesson instead: Egypt, the wilderness, and their own house, all held back from ruin for one reason, God's name.
A sword is sharpened and polished, a king casts lots at a fork in the road, and a profane prince is told his day has come.
Ezekiel is appointed prosecutor of his own city, walks its sins down the social order, and hears of a search for one man to stand in the gap.
Two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, carry Samaria and Jerusalem's story in the book's hardest allegory, told whole and judged in open court.

t: The Pot and the Desire of Your Eyes
d: On the day the siege begins, a cooking pot preaches Jerusalem's end, and the desire of Ezekiel's eyes is taken in a single evening.
The word turns outward: Ammon's cheer, Moab's sneer, Edom's vengeance, and the Philistines' ancient grudge each receive their sentence.
Tyre laughed at Jerusalem's fall and gets three chapters: her walls unbuilt stone by stone until she is a bare rock for spreading nets.
A funeral song for a living city reads Tyre's cargo manifest like a list of the dead, then an east wind breaks the great ship on the high seas.

t: I Am a God; the Guardian Cherub
d: A prince who called himself a god, a king pictured in Eden beside a guardian cherub, and a short, settled word for Israel close the Tyre oracles.
Egypt is a monster in his own river, hooked and hauled out, and the latest-dated oracle in the book pays Babylon's wages in Egyptian land.
A day of clouds for Egypt: fire, shattered allies, a roll of famous cities, and Pharaoh's arm broken a second time, beyond setting.

t: The Cedar in Eden and the Tour of the Pit
d: A cedar that towered over Eden explains Egypt's fall, and the last lament walks Pharaoh down into the Pit to lie among the empires already there.
The watchman charter is preached again to a changed audience, a runner arrives from Jerusalem, and Ezekiel's mouth is opened at last.
God audits the shepherds who fed themselves, dismisses them, and promises the flock one shepherd, His servant David, and a covenant of peace.
Mount Seir is sentenced for gloating over an empty land, and the mountains of Israel, in the same breath, are promised branches, fruit, and people.

t: A New Heart and a New Spirit
d: The greatest promise in the book: not for Israel's sake but for God's name, clean water, a new heart, and His Spirit put within them.
A valley of very dry bones, two sermons preached to bones and breath, and a promise the text itself interprets: these bones are the whole house of Israel.
Two sticks become one in the prophet's hand, one nation under one king, with God's sanctuary in their midst and His covenant of peace forever.
Out of the far north comes Gog against a restored, unwalled land, and the invasion exists, God says, so that the nations may know Him.
Seven years of burning weapons and seven months of burial clear Gog's battlefield, and the book's restoration ends with God's face hidden no longer.
In the twenty-fifth year of exile a man of bronze with a measuring reed walks Ezekiel through walls, gates, and courts, and the tour keeps climbing.
The sound of rushing waters returns from the east: the glory enters by the gate it left, and the throne declares it will never depart again.

t: The Shut Gate and the Sons of Zadok
d: The east gate stays shut because God has entered through it, failed priests are demoted, and the sons of Zadok receive a stricter, linen code.
The country is drawn around the sanctuary, the princes are told enough, and the last laws keep the throne from ever taking a small man's inheritance.
Water trickles from the temple threshold, deepens past measuring, and heals the Dead Sea, while the swamps are honestly left to salt.
The land is divided band by band, foreigners inherit beside native-born sons, and the last measurement of the book becomes a name: the LORD Is There.
Four exiles at the king's table refuse the royal food, and a ten-day test begins a career that outlasts Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar demands the dream itself, the wise men fail, and Daniel's night prayer stops an execution.
A statue of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, a stone cut without hands, and the kingdom that will never be destroyed.

t: The Image of Gold and the Furnace
d: A golden image ninety feet high, three men who will not bow, and a fourth figure walking in the furnace.

t: The King's Letter: A Tree in the Midst of the Land
d: Nebuchadnezzar's own letter tells of a great tree, a watcher, and a stump left banded in the ground.

t: Until You Acknowledge That Heaven Rules
d: Twelve months of warning run out on a palace roof, and the king goes out to pasture until he looks up.
Temple vessels at a feast, a hand writing on the wall, and a kingdom weighed and divided in one night.
A decree Daniel cannot obey, an upper room with open windows, and a king who spends the night fasting.
Daniel dreams now: four beasts from the sea, a court of fire, and One like the Son of Man given forever.

t: The Saints of the Most High
d: The interpretation: a horn at war with the saints, a court that convenes, and a kingdom given to a people.

t: The Ram, the Goat, and Gabriel
d: A ram, a goat flying without touching the ground, and Gabriel sent to explain the time of the end.
An old man reads Jeremiah's seventy years and answers with the longest confession in his book.
Gabriel outruns the prayer and trades seventy years for seventy sevens, counted to a Messiah cut off.
Three weeks of mourning by the Tigris, a man in linen, and a war in heaven that delayed the answer.

t: Kings of the South and the North
d: The Book of Truth read aloud: kings of the South and North, a despicable king, and a sanctuary desecrated.

t: The King Who Exalts Himself, and the End of Days
d: A king who magnifies himself, Michael rising, the dead awakening, and Daniel promised his inheritance.
Sixteen years home, God's house still in ruins, and a prophet sent to audit a pierced bag.
One sermon, three weeks of considering, and the work begins on the twenty-fourth day.

t: The Latter Glory of This House
d: The old men remember Solomon's glory; heaven answers with a shaking and a greater glory to come.

t: From This Day On, I Will Bless You
d: A ruling from the priests, a blessing dated over bare branches, and a signet ring restored.
Two months after Haggai's first sermon, a second prophet opens with the fathers' history and one offer: return to Me.

t: The Horsemen Among the Myrtle Trees
d: A night of visions begins with riders among the myrtles, a world at rest, and an angel asking how long.

t: Four Horns, Four Craftsmen, and a Measuring Line
d: Horns that scattered, craftsmen sent to throw them down, and a city too full for walls with a wall of fire around it.

t: A Firebrand Snatched from the Fire
d: The high priest stands accused in filthy clothes, and the LORD rebukes the accuser and reclothes the priest.

t: Not by Might nor by Power
d: A golden lampstand fed by two olive trees, a mountain made a plain, and the day of small things watched by heaven.

t: The Flying Scroll and the Basket
d: A flying scroll searches the houses of the land, and Wickedness is sealed in a basket and carried to Shinar.
The night's last vision sends out chariots, and by day a crown is set on Joshua's head as a sign of the Branch.

t: Was It for Me That You Fasted?
d: A delegation asks whether to keep fasting, and the answer asks what the fasting was ever for.

t: Old Men and Children in the Streets
d: Short oracles of a city restored: old people in the streets, children playing, fasts turned into feasts.

t: Your King Comes, Riding on a Donkey
d: A burden marches down the map of the nations, and in the middle of it a humble King rides in on a donkey.
Ask the LORD for rain: shepherds judged, a scattered flock whistled home, and a people strengthened in His name.
Zechariah shepherds a flock marked for slaughter, breaks two staffs, and is paid thirty pieces of silver.

t: Look on Me, the One They Have Pierced
d: Jerusalem becomes a heavy stone for the nations, and the delivered city looks on the One they have pierced.

t: A Fountain Opened, a Shepherd Struck
d: A fountain opened for cleansing, false prophets ashamed, and a sword awakened against God's own Shepherd.
The Mount of Olives splits, living water flows from Jerusalem, and HOLY TO THE LORD is written on the horses' bells.
A plague of locusts strips the land, and Joel's first command is to remember it and pass it on.
The ruined fields become a preview of the Day of the LORD, and an army appears at dawn.
Yet even now: the LORD calls His people to return with all their heart.
The LORD spares His people, restores the land, and promises to pour out His Spirit on all people.

t: Multitudes in the Valley of Decision
d: The nations are gathered for judgment, and the book ends with the LORD dwelling in Zion.
The last prophet opens with God's declaration of love and a tired people's question: How have You loved us?
The priests offer blind and lame animals, and God holds them up against the covenant of Levi.
One Father, one covenant, and a people breaking faith at home, with God as witness to every marriage.
To people asking where the God of justice is, God promises a messenger and a refiner's fire.
Return to Me: a call to bring the full tithe and test the LORD's promise of blessing.
God remembers those who fear Him, promises the sun of righteousness, and sends Elijah before the great Day.
Nine chapters of names read as what they are: the roll of a people home from exile, proving the story never broke.
Saul's verdict, the men who gathered to David, and the ark carried up the second time, the right way, with music.

t: The Census and the Threshing Floor
d: Satan incites a census, seventy thousand fall, and the plague stops over a threshing floor that becomes the temple site.

t: Preparing a House He Would Not Build
d: Barred from building, David stockpiles the materials and staffs the entire temple service before a stone is laid.

t: The Plan in Writing and the King's Prayer
d: David hands Solomon a plan he says God put in writing, then gives his own fortune and prays over the nation's willing gifts.
The temple rises on Moriah, the singers praise with one voice, the cloud fills the house, and fire answers the dedication prayer.

t: The Levites Come South, and Abijah Preaches
d: The kingdom splits, the priests and Levites migrate to Jerusalem, Rehoboam humbles himself, and Abijah preaches a battle before fighting it.

t: Asa: The Prayer and the Prison
d: Asa wins a hopeless battle with one prayer, swears a national covenant, and ends by imprisoning the prophet who rebukes him.
Jehoshaphat sends teachers with the Book of the Law through every town, survives Ahab's war, and builds courts that judge for the LORD.
Faced with a vast army, Jehoshaphat prays, a Levite answers, and the choir marches in front of the soldiers.
Elijah's only letter condemns a fratricide king, Jehoiada saves the royal line, and his son is stoned in the temple court.

t: The Censer and the Shut Doors
d: Amaziah's hundred talents, Uzziah's leprosy at the altar, Oded's mercy to captives, and Ahaz locking the temple doors.
Hezekiah reopens his father's shut temple, the song of the LORD restarts, and a second-month Passover invites the north home.

t: The King Who Repented in Chains, and the Last Word
d: Manasseh humbles himself in Babylon and is heard, the messengers are mocked until wrath is beyond remedy, and Cyrus opens the door home.
A Persian king's decree sends the exiles home, and the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar stole are counted out to go back with them.

t: The Names of Those Who Came Up
d: The first return written as a register: 42,360 people, family by family and town by town, including the families who could not prove their names.

t: The Altar and the Weeping Foundation
d: The altar is rebuilt and the feasts resume before the temple has a foundation, and when the foundation is laid, joy and weeping rise in one sound.
A refused partnership turns into hired counselors and royal letters, and the work on the house of God is stopped by force.
Two prophets restart the work, a governor writes a fair report, and everything rides on whether a dead king's decree can be found in the archives.

t: The House Finished and the Passover Kept
d: Darius finds Cyrus' scroll, funds the work from the royal treasury, and the finished house is dedicated and Passover is kept with joy.

t: The Scribe Who Set His Heart
d: Many years later, a scribe who set his heart to study the Law, practice it, and teach it comes up from Babylon carrying a king's letter.
Ezra's company fasts at the Ahava instead of asking for soldiers, and the treasure is weighed out at the river and weighed in at the house.

t: The Prayer at the Evening Offering
d: The leaders' report of mixed marriages drives Ezra to his knees, and his prayer confesses everything and asks for nothing.
A covenant is sworn, an assembly trembles in the rain, an investigation sits for three months, and the book ends on its list.

t: The Queen Who Would Not Come
d: Xerxes feasts for 180 days, and Queen Vashti refuses to come. A decree no one can repeal empties the throne.

t: Esther Crowned, and a Deed in the Record
d: An exiled orphan is crowned queen, and her cousin's deed at the gate is written into a book nobody reads. Yet.
Haman rises, Mordecai will not bow, and the lot picks a day for a people's destruction.
Sackcloth at the gate, messages through a eunuch, and a queen decides: if I perish, I perish.

t: The First Banquet and the Gallows
d: The scepter is extended, the request is deferred, and a gallows fifty cubits high goes up in the night.
The king cannot sleep, the chronicles are read, and Haman parades the man he came to hang.
At the second banquet the queen names the enemy, and the gallows finds its man.
Haman's ring changes hands, a second decree answers the first, and Susa shouts.

t: Purim: The Days That Were Turned
d: The day is overturned, the plunder is refused three times, and Purim enters the calendar forever.
A brother's report from Judah breaks a cupbearer's heart in Susa, and his prayer ends by asking for mercy in the sight of one particular man.

t: The King's Question and the Night Ride
d: A sad face before the king, a prayer breathed in half a second, and a midnight ride around the ruins before a word is spoken to anyone.
The record of the builders, gate by gate: priests and perfumers, a ruler's daughters, and the nobles who would not stoop.
A fox joke, a conspiracy, and a workforce rebuilt as a garrison, building with a weapon in one hand.
The famine inside the wall: fields mortgaged, children enslaved, a shaken robe, and a governor who would not eat the governor's bread.
Four invitations, an unsealed letter, a hired prophet, and a wall finished in fifty-two days.

t: A City to Fill, and the Register
d: Guards at the gates, an empty city, and the old register of the first return found and opened for a new purpose.
A platform in the square, six hours of reading, weeping turned to feasting, and booths built for the first time since Joshua.
Sackcloth and dust, and the whole history of Israel prayed back to God by the Levites, ending here we are as slaves.
The covenant in writing: marriages, Sabbath, debts, wood, firstfruits, and tithes, under one resolve, not to neglect the house of God.

t: One of Ten, and Two Choirs
d: The lot that filled the city, and two thanksgiving choirs circling the finished wall in opposite directions to meet in the house of God.
The governor returns to find Tobiah in the storeroom, the Levites in their fields, and the Sabbath for sale, and ends his book with a prayer.

t: The Greatest Man of the East
d: A blameless man loses everything in one day, and blesses God anyway.
The attack reaches Job's own body, his wife urges him to curse God, and three friends come to sit with him.

t: May the Day of My Birth Perish
d: After seven silent days, Job opens his mouth and curses the day he was born.
Eliphaz answers with a night vision and an old doctrine: the innocent do not perish.
Job calls his friends faithless streams and asks God why He will not pardon him.
Bildad explains the children's deaths, and Job asks for a mediator who does not exist.
Job loathes his life and begs for the charge sheet; Zophar answers that God could demand more.
Job declares he will hope in God though He slay him, and wonders if a man will live again.

t: Eliphaz Returns, and Job's Witness in Heaven
d: Eliphaz repeats the doctrine harder, and Job claims a witness and an advocate in heaven.
Bildad describes the wicked man's trap, and Job answers with the Redeemer who lives.

t: Zophar, and Why the Wicked Live On
d: Zophar says the wicked triumph briefly; Job asks why they live on, growing old and increasing in power.

t: Eliphaz Names Sins, and Job Seeks God's Seat
d: Eliphaz names specific sins the book never shows, and Job longs to plead his case at God's seat.

t: Bildad's Six Verses and the Search for Wisdom
d: Bildad's last speech is six verses; Job answers with a hymn and the great poem asking where wisdom can be found.

t: The Signature: Job's Oath of Innocence
d: Job remembers the gate where he defended the poor, swears his oath of innocence charge by charge, and signs it.
A young man who has listened to the whole debate burns with anger at both sides and claims God speaks through suffering.

t: Elihu: God Is Great, Beyond Our Knowledge
d: Elihu finishes inside a rising storm, telling Job to stand still and consider the wonders of God.

t: Where Were You? The LORD Answers
d: God answers out of the whirlwind, questioning Job about the foundations of the earth and the wild animals.
Job places his hand over his mouth, and God presents two creatures no man can master.

t: Now My Eyes Have Seen You
d: Job has seen God, the friends are rebuked and forgiven through his prayer, and his latter days are blessed more than his first.
The book names its purpose, a father warns his son off the gang’s road, and Wisdom calls in the street.
Wisdom must be dug for like silver, and the man who finds her learns trust, correction, and generosity.
A father’s inherited teaching: guard the heart, for from it flow the springs of life.

t: The Ant, the Fire, and the Snare
d: The ant schools the slacker, seven things are named that the LORD hates, and a young man drifts into the snare.
Wisdom stands at the crossroads and tells who she is: older than the hills, at God’s side in creation.
Two houses, two invitations, one street: Wisdom’s feast against Folly’s stolen water.

t: The Proverbs of Solomon: Two Ways
d: Solomon’s sayings begin: two ways weighed in couplets of mouths, hands, and honest scales.
A gentle answer, a weighed heart, and the warning that pride goes before destruction.

t: Life and Death in the Power of the Tongue
d: Life and death in the power of the tongue, kindness to the poor as a loan to the LORD, and a good name.

t: The Thirty Sayings of the Wise
d: The words of the wise: thirty sayings guarding the poor, the drunkard’s woe, and a sluggard’s ruined vineyard.

t: Copied by the Men of Hezekiah
d: Sayings copied by Hezekiah’s men: the fool answered and not answered, iron sharpening iron, mercy for the confessed.

t: Agur: I Am Weary, O God
d: Agur confesses his ignorance, prays for neither poverty nor riches, and learns from ants and eagles.

t: Lemuel, and the Wife of Noble Character
d: A mother’s teaching for a king, and the book’s closing portrait of the wife of noble character.
The Teacher states his verdict, watches the world's circles, and reports his first experiment: wisdom itself.

t: The Test of Pleasure and Work
d: Pleasure, building, and greatness are tested at royal scale, and the first joy refrain answers the despair.
The seasons poem stands whole, eternity sits in the heart, and man and beast go to one dust.
Oppression without a comforter, envy as the engine of toil, and the threefold cord against the lone man.
Few words before God, vows paid, money that never satisfies, and wealth a stranger enjoys.
The better sayings, prosperity and adversity from one hand, and the search that could not fathom.

t: Time and Chance Happen to Them All
d: The wicked praised at their graves, the great inversion, one fate for all, and the forgotten poor wise man.
The last sayings, the ventures of faith, the aging poem, and the book's own conclusion about the whole matter.
Her voice opens the book: longing for the king, dark and lovely under the sun, and the first charge to the daughters.
He comes leaping over the mountains with the spring call, and the first night search ends in finding and holding.
Solomon's procession, the bride praised feature by feature, the locked garden opened, and the friends' blessing.

t: I Opened to My Beloved, but He Had Gone
d: A knock in the night, a door opened too late, the watchmen's blows, and her praise of the one she cannot find.
His praise renewed above queens and concubines, the Shulammite called back, and the belonging line in its final form.

t: Let Us Go to the Countryside
d: Her dawn invitation to the vineyards, the wish about a brother, and love declared as strong as death.

t: My Own Vineyard Is Mine to Give
d: The brothers' plan for the little sister, her answer, the vineyard accounts settled, and her voice last.

t: The Son of David, the Son of Abraham
d: The family line rolls down forty-two generations to Joseph, an angel's dream, and a name given before the birth.

t: Wise Men, a Flight, and Weeping in Ramah
d: Magi from the east, a king's lie, a night flight to Egypt, Bethlehem's grief, and a quiet homecoming to Nazareth.

t: Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven Is Near
d: John preaches at the Jordan, points past himself, and baptizes the one whose sandals he is unworthy to carry.
Forty days hungry in the wilderness, three tests, and every answer drawn from the written word.
The light rises in Galilee, four fishermen drop their nets, and the crowds begin to gather.

t: Blessed Are the Poor in Spirit
d: The sermon opens: blessings for the unlikely, righteousness deeper than the scribes', and love for enemies.

t: Your Father Who Sees What Is Done in Secret
d: Giving, prayer, and fasting before an audience of one, the prayer Jesus taught, and the answer to worry.
The sermon closes: beams and specks, the Father's generosity, two ways, two builders, and astonished crowds.
A leper touched, a centurion's faith, a storm stilled, and a town that begged its deliverer to leave.
A paralytic forgiven and walking, a tax collector called, two rescues interlocked, and sheep without a shepherd.
The twelve are named and sent with a charge that darkens into warnings, promises, and a cup of cold water.

t: Come to Me, All You Who Are Weary
d: A prophet's doubt from prison, woes on the towns that saw the miracles, and the most open invitation in the Bible.
Sabbath collisions, the servant song, the Beelzebul charge, and family redefined around the Father's will.
Seven parables of the kingdom by the sea, and a hometown that could see only the carpenter's son.

t: A Prophet Without Honor, and Five Thousand Fed
d: A prophet's head on a platter, five thousand fed in grief's shadow, and a hand holding Peter up out of the sea.

t: What Comes Out of the Mouth
d: Tradition against command, a Canaanite mother's crumbs, and bread multiplied on the far side of the border.
Leaven warned against, the great confession at Caesarea Philippi, and the cross named in the same hour.

t: This Is My Beloved Son; Listen to Him
d: Glory on the mountain, failure at its foot, a second prediction, and a coin in a fish's mouth.
The church's rule of life: greatness measured by descent, the lost sheep sought, and forgiveness without arithmetic.
Divorce taken back to Genesis, children welcomed, a rich man walking away sad, and a camel at the needle's eye.
A vineyard queue run backwards, a cup the brothers do not understand, and two blind men who would not be silenced.

t: Hosanna to the Son of David
d: A king on a donkey's colt, tables overturned, a fig tree withered, and a question the authorities dared not answer.
Indictment parables in the temple, traps about taxes and resurrection, and the two commandments everything hangs on.
Seven woes on the religious establishment, and the prosecutor's voice breaking over the city he longed to gather.

t: Not One Stone Left on Another
d: The last discourse: birth pains, tribulation, the coming of the Son of Man, and one command, keep watch.
Oil for the wait, talents at risk, and a King who counts a meal and a prison visit as service to himself.
Perfume and thirty pieces of silver, a last Passover remade, prayers in a garden, and an arrest by a kiss.

t: Before the Council, and Peter in the Courtyard
d: Two trials in parallel: a prisoner who confesses under oath, a disciple who denies by a fire, and a betrayer's end.
Washed hands, a crown of thorns, a charge nailed up as the truth, and the verdict spoken by the executioner.
A rich man's tomb, a guard the opposition requested, an empty grave at dawn, and a mountain in Galilee.
No genealogy, no manger: Mark opens with Isaiah's voice, John at the Jordan, and Jesus driven into the wilderness.
The kingdom sermon, four fishermen called mid-task, a synagogue amazed, and a leper whose news drives Jesus into the desert.

t: The Son of Man Has Authority on Earth
d: A paralytic lowered through a roof, a tax collector called, the fasting question, and two Sabbaths that end in a murder plot.
Crowds at the sea, twelve names appointed, the Beelzebul charge answered, and the family of Jesus redrawn at a doorway.
The sower and the soils, the lamp, the seed growing while the farmer sleeps, and the smallest seed of all.
A storm stilled, a legion sent into the sea, a woman healed by a touch, and a twelve-year-old raised with two Aramaic words.
Nazareth takes offense, the Twelve are sent out with a staff, and Herod's banquet ends with the Baptist's head on a platter.
Five loaves feed five thousand, Jesus walks on the sea past his own disciples, and a whole region begs for the fringe of his cloak.

t: Their Hearts Are Far from Me
d: Tradition against commandment, a Syrophoenician mother who will not leave empty, and a deaf man's ears opened with a sigh.
A second feeding, a refused sign, a boat full of men who cannot do the arithmetic, and a blind man healed in two stages.
Peter confesses the Christ and rebukes him in the same hour, the cross is named a follower's road, and glory breaks out on a mountain.

t: If Anyone Wants to Be First
d: A father's honest prayer, a second prediction nobody understands, an argument about greatness, and a child set in the middle.

t: Let the Children Come to Me
d: Marriage from Eden, children blessed, a rich man who goes away sad, thrones requested, and Bartimaeus who follows on the road.
A colt, a cheering crowd, a fruitless fig tree, a temple cleared, and a question about authority answered with a question.
Tenants who kill the son, Caesar's coin, a resurrection riddle undone, the greatest commandment, and a widow's two coins.
The temple doomed, wars and witness, the abomination of desolation, the Son of Man coming in clouds, and a doorkeeper told to stay awake.

t: One of You Will Betray Me
d: A jar of nard broken open, Judas gone to the priests, a last Passover, and a rooster prophesied before midnight.

t: My Soul Is Overwhelmed with Sorrow
d: Gethsemane's prayer, three sleepers, a kiss in the garden, a silent prisoner who finally says I am, and Peter weeping in a courtyard.
Pilate's questions, Barabbas chosen, the long road to Golgotha, darkness at noon, and a centurion who says what no one else has.
Women at dawn, an empty tomb, a message naming Peter, the fear that ends the earliest text, and the received ending that sends the story worldwide.
Luke opens like an investigator, then takes us into the temple, where an old priest hears the first good news in four hundred years and comes out unable to speak.
Gabriel visits a young woman in Nazareth, the Spirit overshadows her, and two mothers meet in the hill country with a song on the younger one's lips.
A baby is named by a written word, a silenced father's mouth opens, and his song runs from his own house to the sunrise from on high.
An emperor's decree moves a family to Bethlehem, and the announcement of the birth goes first to shepherds on the night watch.
Simeon and Anna recognize the child in the temple, and twelve years later his parents find him there again, among the teachers.

t: Prepare the Way for the Lord
d: John preaches repentance at the Jordan, answers the crowds' question with specifics, and points past himself to the stronger One.

t: The Son of Adam, the Son of God
d: Heaven opens over the praying Jesus, and Luke traces his line upward past Abraham and David all the way to Adam, and to God.
Full of the Spirit and led by the Spirit, Jesus faces three offers in the desert and answers each from Deuteronomy, ending at Jerusalem's height.
A Nazareth sermon ends at a cliff edge, demons are silenced in Capernaum, and a failed night's fishing becomes the call of the first disciples.
A leper is touched, a paralytic is lowered through a roof, a tax collector hosts a feast, and the new wine bursts the old arrangements.
Grain plucked on the Sabbath, a withered hand restored in full view, a night of prayer, and twelve apostles named at morning.

t: Blessed Are You Who Are Poor
d: On a level place the blessings come with matching woes, love of enemies is commanded, and the sermon ends with two foundations.

t: Young Man, I Say to You, Arise
d: A centurion's faith amazes Jesus without a meeting, and a widow's only son sits up in his coffin at a word.

t: Her Many Sins Have Been Forgiven
d: John sends a question from prison, Jesus defends the Baptist and weeps over a generation, and a sinful woman washes his feet with her tears.
The women who fund the ministry are named, the sower's seed falls on four soils, and Jesus redraws the boundaries of family.

t: Do Not Be Afraid; Only Believe
d: A storm is stilled, a legion is drowned, a bleeding woman is named daughter, and a twelve-year-old is told to get up.
The Twelve are sent out with nothing, Herod is perplexed, and five loaves feed five thousand men beside Bethsaida.

t: Who Do You Say I Am?
d: Peter confesses the Christ of God, glory breaks out on the mountain, and the road south demands everything from those who would follow.
Seventy-two are sent two by two, woes fall on the lake towns, and the returning messengers learn where joy really lives.
A lawyer's test becomes the parable of the Samaritan, and a busy hostess learns the one thing necessary at Jesus' feet.
Luke's own Lord's Prayer, a midnight knock, the finger of God, and a warning about the light within.
A dinner turns into six woes, leaven is named hypocrisy, and a rich fool's full barns meet their owner's last night.
Ravens and lilies argue against worry, the little flock is promised the kingdom, and watchful servants keep their lamps burning.
Disasters are refused as verdicts, a bent woman is loosed on the Sabbath, and the journeying Jesus laments over Jerusalem like a hen over chicks.
Seats at a Pharisee's table are rearranged by a parable, invited guests excuse themselves out of a feast, and the cost of discipleship is counted.
A sheep, a coin, and a son: three lost things, three searches, and a father pleading with the son who stayed home.
A shrewd manager spends his last authority well, money's limits are stated, and a beggar at a gate is named where a rich man is not.
Forgiveness seven times a day, ten lepers cleansed and one foreigner back, the kingdom in their midst, and two men praying in the temple.

t: What Must I Do to Inherit Eternal Life?
d: Children are welcomed, a rich ruler goes away sad, the third prediction is not understood, and a blind beggar sees and follows.

t: To Seek and to Save the Lost
d: A chief tax collector comes down from a tree a changed man, and a nobleman's minas test his servants while the kingdom delays.
A borrowed colt, a shouting multitude, tears over Jerusalem, and a temple cleared to be a house of prayer again.

t: He Is Not the God of the Dead
d: Authority challenged and returned, tenants who kill the son, Caesar's coin, and the resurrection proved from the burning bush.

t: Heaven and Earth Will Pass Away
d: A widow's two coins outweigh a treasury, the temple's stones are doomed, and the disciples are told to stand up and lift their heads.
Judas agrees on a price, the Passover is prepared, the body and the cup are given, and Peter is promised a turning back before he falls.
Sweat like drops of blood, an ear healed in the arresting crowd, three denials by a courtyard fire, and a council that convicts on his own words.
Herod gets no word at all, Pilate finds no guilt three times, and the crowd's clamor prevails over both courts.
A prayer for the executioners, a criminal promised Paradise today, darkness at noon, and a borrowed tomb before the Sabbath.
Women disbelieved, Peter wondering, and two travelers who recognize the stranger only when he breaks the bread.
Flesh and bones and broiled fish, minds opened to the Scriptures, a blessing interrupted by heaven, and joy back in the temple.

t: In the Beginning Was the Word
d: Before the manger and the genealogy, John's Gospel opens in eternity, with the Word who was with God and was God.
A priestly delegation interrogates John the Baptist, and the next day he points at Jesus and gives him his first public title.
The first disciples come to Jesus one by one, each brought by somebody else, and Nathanael is undone by a fig tree.
At a wedding in Cana the wine runs out, and Jesus turns six jars of wash water into the finest wine of the feast.
At his first Passover Jesus clears the temple courts with a whip and answers the demand for a sign with a riddle about three days.
Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, comes to Jesus at night and hears that seeing the kingdom requires a second birth.
John the Baptist answers his disciples' jealousy with the joy of the bridegroom's friend: he must increase, I must decrease.
At Jacob's well at noon, Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink and tells her about living water and true worship.

t: The Fields Are White for Harvest
d: The woman leaves her jar and evangelizes her town, while Jesus tells his disciples the fields are already ripe.
A royal official begs Jesus to come and heal his dying son, and takes him at his word across twenty miles.
By the pool of Bethesda Jesus heals a man invalid for thirty-eight years, on the Sabbath, and the persecution begins.
Jesus answers the charge of making himself equal with God: the Son gives life, judges, and calls his witnesses.
Five barley loaves feed five thousand on the hillside, and that night Jesus walks across the stormy sea to his disciples.

t: I Am the Bread of Life
d: The crowd that ate the loaves demands another sign, and Jesus declares himself the bread that came down from heaven.
The hard saying about eating his flesh empties the crowd, and Peter confesses there is nowhere else to go.
At the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus teaches in the temple, the crowd divides, the officers return empty-handed, and Nicodemus speaks up.
A woman caught in adultery is dragged before Jesus as a test, and her accusers walk away one by one, oldest first.

t: I Am the Light of the World
d: In the temple courts Jesus debates his testimony, his father, and Abraham, until he says the words that bring out the stones.
Jesus gives sight to a man born blind, and the healed beggar out-argues the council that throws him out of the synagogue.
Jesus pictures the sheepfold: thieves climb the wall, but the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
At the Feast of Dedication Jesus says, I and the Father are one, escapes the stones, and withdraws across the Jordan.

t: I Am the Resurrection and the Life
d: Word comes that Lazarus is sick; Jesus waits two days, then meets Martha on the road outside Bethany.
At the tomb Jesus weeps, calls Lazarus out of the grave, and the Sanhedrin resolves that one man must die for the nation.
Mary anoints Jesus' feet with costly perfume, the crowds come to see Lazarus too, and Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey.
Greeks ask to see Jesus, a voice speaks from heaven, and John's Gospel closes out the public ministry with Isaiah's audit.

t: He Loved Them to the End
d: At the last supper Jesus washes his disciples' feet, gives the morsel to Judas, and tells Peter about the rooster.
The farewell begins: many rooms, the way and the truth and the life, another Advocate, and a peace the world cannot give.
On the road to the garden Jesus pictures the vine and the branches, renames servants as friends, and warns of the world's hatred.
The farewell ends with sorrow turned to joy, the promise of plain speech, and a victory spoken in the past tense.
Jesus prays aloud for himself, for the eleven, and for everyone who will ever believe through their message.
In the garden Jesus steps forward and is bound; inside Annas's courtyard, Peter warms himself and denies him three times.
Before Pilate, Jesus speaks of a kingdom not of this world, is flogged and mocked, and is handed over when the priests claim Caesar.
Jesus carries his own cross, provides for his mother, finishes the work, and is buried by Joseph and Nicodemus in a garden tomb.
Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty, meets the risen Lord in the garden, and Thomas moves from conditions to the Gospel's highest confession.
By the Sea of Tiberias the risen Jesus cooks breakfast, restores Peter beside a charcoal fire, and the Gospel signs its name.
Luke opens his second volume where his Gospel ended: forty days of the risen Jesus, one command to wait, and a promise that maps the whole book.
The praying church fills Judas's empty place by lot, restoring the twelve witnesses before the Spirit comes.
On Pentecost the Spirit fills the house with wind and fire, and Galileans declare God's wonders in the languages of the world.
Peter's first sermon runs from Joel's prophecy to the empty tomb, and three thousand are baptized before the day ends.
Luke's first summary of the church's life: teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer, with the Lord adding daily.
Peter and John have no silver or gold, but a man lame from birth walks into the temple in the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

t: The God of Abraham Has Glorified His Servant
d: Over the healed beggar, Peter preaches the Author of life to the crowd in Solomon's Colonnade and calls them to repent.
Before the Sanhedrin, Peter names Jesus the cornerstone and declares there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved.
The threatened church prays for boldness instead of safety, the place shakes, and Barnabas lays a field's price at the apostles' feet.

t: You Have Lied to the Holy Spirit
d: Ananias and Sapphira stage a generosity they did not practice, and the young church learns that the Spirit in the room is not safe to counterfeit.
An angel redeploys the jailed apostles to the temple courts, Gamaliel counsels the council to wait, and the flogged men leave rejoicing.
A complaint about the widows' food line produces the Seven, all Greek names, chosen by the church and ordained with prayer.
Arrested on arranged charges, Stephen answers with Israel's whole history: Abraham, Joseph, and Moses, the rejected deliverer sent back as redeemer.

t: Lord, Do Not Hold This Sin Against Them
d: The defense becomes an indictment, Stephen sees the Son of Man standing, and the first martyr dies praying for his executioners while Saul watches.
Persecution scatters the church into its second field; Philip preaches in Samaria, and Simon the sorcerer tries to buy the Holy Spirit.

t: What Prevents Me from Being Baptized?
d: On a desert road, Philip opens Isaiah for Ethiopia's treasurer, and the ends of the earth believe in a single chariot.
The persecutor with warrants meets the risen Jesus on the Damascus road and is baptized by a disciple brave enough to call him brother.
Saul preaches in Damascus, escapes in a basket, is vouched for by Barnabas in Jerusalem, and the church enjoys a season of peace.
Peter heals Aeneas at Lydda and raises Tabitha at Joppa, staying on in the house of a tanner named Simon.

t: A Sheet Let Down from Heaven
d: A Roman centurion's prayer is answered in Joppa, where a hungry Peter sees a sheet full of animals and hears a voice he argues with.
Peter preaches in Cornelius's house, and the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles mid-sermon, before the water, before the vote.
Peter defends the Gentile mission in Jerusalem, nameless believers found the church at Antioch, and Barnabas fetches Saul from Tarsus.
Herod kills James and jails Peter; an angel walks Peter out past the guards, Rhoda forgets to open the gate, and Herod falls in Caesarea.
In a worshiping, fasting church at Antioch, the Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul; on Cyprus a sorcerer goes blind and a governor believes.
Paul's synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch ends with the journey's charter: since you reject it, we turn to the Gentiles.
At Lystra a healed cripple brings sacrifice to the apostles, then stones Paul; the first journey closes with elders appointed in every church.
The circumcision question is settled by testimony, prophecy, and a short letter: it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.
Paul and Barnabas part over Mark, Timothy is circumcised for the road, a Macedonian pleads in a vision, and Lydia's heart is opened at Philippi.
A slave girl's deliverance lands Paul and Silas in the stocks; they sing, the earth shakes, and the jailer's household is baptized before dawn.
Thessalonica charges the missionaries with treason for naming another king, and the Bereans check the Scriptures daily to see if it is true.
In Athens Paul preaches from an altar to an unknown god to the Areopagus, and a handful believe, including a member of the council.
Paul works at a Corinth workbench for a year and a half under a vision's promise, and Gallio dismisses his case without hearing his defense.
Priscilla and Aquila take an eloquent Alexandrian aside and explain the way of God more accurately, and Apollos sails to Achaia with a letter.
Two years in Tyrannus's hall, a fortune in magic books burned, and a silversmith's riot that a city clerk dissolves; Paul resolves to see Rome.

t: You Will Not See My Face Again
d: Eutychus falls and is restored at Troas, and on the beach at Miletus Paul charges Ephesus's elders and kneels with them in tears.
Warnings follow Paul up the coast; Agabus binds himself with Paul's belt, James proposes a vow, and a mob drags Paul out of the temple.
From the fortress steps Paul tells Jerusalem his story in Hebrew until one word, Gentiles, breaks the hearing; his citizenship stops the flogging.
Paul splits the Sanhedrin on resurrection, a nephew exposes the ambush, and 470 soldiers carry him by night to Caesarea with Lysias's letter.
Before Felix the case dissolves into adjournment and bribery hopes; before Festus, Paul exercises a citizen's right and appeals to Caesar.
Paul's longest defense retells Damascus to a king, Festus cries madness, Agrippa asks about a short persuasion, and the verdict is innocence.
A prison ship sails into the Northeaster; fourteen days of storm end with bread given thanks for, a sandbar, and all 276 brought safely to land.
Malta's kindness, a viper shaken off, and Rome at last: two whole years in a rented house, the kingdom preached boldly and freely.
Paul opens with credentials instead of thanksgiving, and curses any gospel but the one first preached.
Paul’s gospel did not come from men: a ruined career, a desert, and fifteen days in Jerusalem, sworn to.
Jerusalem adds nothing and takes Titus uncircumcised; then Peter’s table at Antioch breaks the fellowship.
Justified by faith, not works of law, and Abraham’s blessing reaches the Gentiles through the curse borne on a tree.
The promise predates the law by 430 years; the guardian’s custody ends in adoption and the cry of Abba.
Paul reads Abraham’s two sons as two covenants, and asks which mother the Galatians mean to claim.
Freedom guarded from the flesh, and the Spirit’s ninefold fruit set against the flesh’s charge sheet.
Burdens carried, seed sown, and the letter signed in large letters with one boast left standing.
Three senders, one young church: faith that works, love that labors, hope that endures, and a report that outran the missionaries.
The visit defended from the congregation’s own memory: no flattery, no greed, a nursing mother, a father, and nights of work.
Received as the word of God, imitated in suffering, and a team torn away, calling the converts its crown.
Timothy sent back from Athens, and returned with the news that turns distress into life: they are standing firm.

t: Live in a Way That Is Pleasing to God
d: More and more: a holy body, a love taught by God, and the quiet ambition of working hands.
Grief with hope: the dead in Christ rise first, the living are caught up together, and the words themselves are the comfort.
No times and seasons, but wakefulness: sons of light, armed with faith, love, and the hope of salvation.

t: Hold Fast to What Is Good
d: The ordinary church’s running order, three short commands, tested fire, and a letter ordered to be read to all the brothers.
The same three senders, an obligation of thanksgiving: faith growing, love increasing, and endurance read as evidence.
Relief at the revelation, fire for the afflicters, glory in the saints, and the prayer that fills the interval.
A forged alarm answered: the Day has not come, the rebellion and the lawless one come first, and memory is the cure.

t: Until He Is Taken Out of the Way
d: The restraint the letter never explains, lawlessness already at work, a breath that ends it, and a delusion sent on refusal.
Chosen, called through the gospel, and told to cling: the thanksgiving that answers the storm.
Pray for us, imitate the example, let the unwilling go hungry, admonish the brother, and know the mark in every letter.
A thanksgiving full of grace, then the first report: the church that Paul planted is sorting itself into camps behind its teachers.
One event, two verdicts: to the world a crucified Messiah is foolishness, and God chose the foolish and the weak on purpose.
Paul's trembling preaching, the hidden wisdom the rulers never saw, and the Spirit who knows the thoughts of God.
Infants on milk, servants in a field, builders on one foundation, and a temple the factions are damaging.
Judgment deferred to the Lord, the apostles displayed as the world's refuse, and a father's choice: a rod, or love.
A case the church is proud of instead of grieved by, a little leaven through the whole batch, and an earlier letter corrected.
Brother suing brother before unbelievers, a catalog answered by a past tense, and the body as a temple with a price paid.
The Corinthians' own questions: marriage, singleness, mixed homes, slavery and freedom, and the shortness of the time.

t: Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
d: An idol is nothing, and a brother is not: knowledge that destroys the weak is answered by a man giving up meat forever.

t: Woe to Me If I Do Not Preach
d: Every right of an apostle established from Scripture, and every one of them surrendered; the athlete who can be disqualified.
Israel's privileges and Israel's graveyard, two tables no one can sit at together, and freedom governed by another's conscience.
The traditions carried as written, a Supper that had stopped being shared, and the words of institution against the abuse.
Different gifts, the same Spirit; a body whose members cannot spare each other, arranged by God on purpose.
Every gift weighed without love and found wanting; love described as conduct, and the three that remain.
Intelligibility as the assembly's rule: five coherent words against ten thousand, and everything done in order.
The gospel received and handed on, named witnesses, and the chain that follows if Christ has not been raised.
A seed and its body, splendor fitted to everything, the trumpet, the taunt over death, and work that is not in vain.

t: My Love Be With All of You
d: The collection, the road through Macedonia, Apollos in God's time, and a greeting in Paul's own hand.
